questions.cardText:
[Computer Science] Why is a computer bug called a “bug”?
A. The term was borrowed from aviation engineering
B. Because an actual insect caused an issue in an early computer
C. It was named after a popular comic strip character
Answer: B. In 1947, a moth was found to cause a malfunction in an early computer. It was logged as a “bug.” The logbook with the moth taped to it is now housed in a museum.
questions.en: Which insect, found trapped in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947, was taped into the logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found”?
questions.de: Welches Insekt, das 1947 in einem Relais des Computers Harvard Mark II gefunden wurde, klebte man als „first actual case of bug being found“ ins Logbuch?

timeline.labelEn: Operators of the Harvard Mark II find a moth in a relay and tape it into the logbook
timeline.labelDe: Bediener des Harvard Mark II finden eine Motte in einem Relais und kleben sie ins Logbuch

questions.notes: The card is wrong about the etymology: 'bug' for a technical fault was engineering jargon since at least the 1870s (Edison, 1878); the 1947 moth only made the existing term famous — hence the 'first actual case of bug'. Open question asks the moth fact. The logbook is in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

questions.cardText:
[Engineering and Inventions] What was the first mammal to be cloned from an adult somatic cell?
A. A sheep B. A mouse C. A guinea pig
Answer: A. Dolly the sheep, cloned in 1996, was the first mammal to be cloned from an adult somatic cell.
questions.en: What was the name of the sheep, born in 1996, that was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell?
questions.de: Wie hieß das 1996 geborene Schaf, das als erstes Säugetier aus einer adulten Körperzelle geklont wurde?

timeline.labelEn: Birth of Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell
timeline.labelDe: Geburt des Schafs Dolly, des ersten aus einer adulten Körperzelle geklonten Säugetiers

questions.notes: Card answer (a sheep) confirmed; the open question asks for the sheep's name. Cloned at the Roslin Institute, Scotland, by somatic cell nuclear transfer.
